idiom_name: Hash memo with frozen array keys, key?/[]= as the hit test
implementation_notes: Ruby's memo idiom is a Hash: either Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = compute(k) } or explicit key?/[]= pairs, with [rule_id, pos] array keys - two Arrays are the same key when hash and eql? agree, which the docs state as 'Hash Key Equivalence'. What replaces the classic memo-table object is that the Hash is a plain instance variable and each rule method is two lines: check key?, then on a miss compute and store the result including failures, because Hash#[] returns nil for a missing key and nil/false cannot serve as the failure marker without making the cache ambiguous. Hash.new's default-proc form is the local idiom for the compute-on-miss half, but the proc must assign into the Hash itself or every probe re-evaluates.
pitfalls: @memo[key] ||= compute(key) is not memoization when the result may be nil or false - it recomputes on every call; use key?/fetch or a non-nil failure object.
Modifying a key while it sits in a Hash damages the index (docs: 'Modifying an Active Hash Key'), so position keys must stay frozen/immutable.
A default-proc Hash runs the proc on every missing read, probes included; the proc must assign into the Hash itself, otherwise misses are recomputed and non-mutating probes allocate.
